newsitem.title: UK: Scottish Nationalists promise less tax.
newsitem.headline: Scottish Nationalists promise less tax.

text.p: Nationalists on Monday pledged lower taxes in an general election manifesto which claimed that an independent Scotland would be the industrialised world's eighth richest nation.

"We intend to fight a campaign of head and hearts, of enterprise and compassion, of social concern and economic progress. That is the way we will win freedom for our nation," Scottish National Party (SNP) leader Alex Salmond said.
Opinion polls put SNP support at about 25 percent of Scottish voters, behind Labour at around 50 percent, and the ruling Conservatives at around 20.
But Labour, firm favourites to win the May 1 election, have hit problems with their plans for a regional assembly in Scotland.

Labour intends to hold a referendum by the autumn in Scotland to establish a parliament in Edinburgh that would have the power to vary income tax by as much as three percentage points for Scottish taxpayers.
Labour, however, has firmly ruled out any increase in income tax for the next five years. Blair has been unable satisfactorily to explain this apparent paradox.
"We are winning the arguments, economic and political. Now we must concentrate on winning the election," said Salmond.

Drawing on figures compiled by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, a Paris-based economic forum, the SNP says that, if North Sea oil revenues were taken into account, an independent Scotland would be the eighth richest nation in the developed world. The SNP did not specify whether this was a per capita calculation.
The British government denies Scotland is entitled to its share of oil revenues.

The SNP is tiny in British political terms, having only four of 72 Scottish members in the outgoing 651-seat British parliament. Conservatives held 10 Scottish seats, Labour 49 and Liberal Democrats nine. Salmond said the SNP would gain seats in the May 1 polling but declined to give a figure. "We are Scotland's second-largest party, we intend to be first."
The latest poll found 36 percent of Scots wanted independence from England with 35 percent wanting a separate parliament within the United Kingdom.
Just 24 percent wanted the 290-year-old union of England and Scotland to remain unchanged.
"Elections are not won on opinion polls," Salmond told reporters. "They are won on the arguments."
The manifesto sets out a radical programme of economic and political change for an independent Scotland.
It calls for a modern single chamber parliament, elected by proportional representation, with the franchise including all over 16, rather than 18 at present.
There would be a written constitution for the first time and a reformed monarchy, keeping the monarch as head of state with reduced duties.
Corporation tax would be cut from 33 to 30 percent, with a small companies rate of 18 percent, to give Scottish business a competitive edge.

Michael Forsyth, the Conservative minister in charge of government in Scotland, castigated the SNP as Europe's most left-wing party since the downfall of communism. It had the most damaging of all the irresponsible programmes set out by opposition parties, he said on Monday.
"Scottish Nationalists threaten our stability, our prosperity and our influence in the world," he said. "Their programme is a blueprint for poverty creation."
